# Introduction

Metal-organic frameworks occupy a privileged position in biomimetic catalysis [@Smith2023].
Their reticular architecture allows chemists to specify pore geometry and local chemistry
with precision unmatched by zeolites or mesoporous silicas [@Jones2024].

The catalytic machinery of enzymes achieves reaction selectivities that synthetic chemists
can rarely match. Central to this performance is the precise three-dimensional arrangement
of residues around a buried active site. Translating these principles into porous solid-state
materials has become one of the defining ambitions of the past decade [@Smith2023; @Jones2024].

Here we argue, from a synthesis of recent crystallographic, spectroscopic, and computational
data, that the operative mechanism is a two-step conformational gating in which framework
flexibility controls access to the catalytic metal node [@Brown2022].
